questions.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3(0.5)^{4n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=3(0.5)^{4(1)}=3(0.5)^{4}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=3(0.5)^{4(2)}=3(0.5)^{8}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{3(0.5)^{8}}{3(0.5)^{4}}=(0.5)^{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3(0.5)^{4n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{3(0.5)^{4}}{1-(0.5)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2(1)}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2(2)}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{4}}{\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}}={(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}=\frac{4}{25}.
$$

 

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}}{1-\frac{4}{25}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{7}{10}(\frac{4}{25})}{\frac{21}{25}} \\  & =\frac{7}{10}\cdot \frac{4}{25}\cdot \frac{25}{21} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Given Its First Term and Common Ratio
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $a_1=-2$ and $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4$ for all integers $n \geq 1,$ find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{n}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <    1,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
a_1=-2.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1-(-0.4)} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1.4} \\  & =-\frac{10}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <    1,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is 

$$
a_1 = 2(0.5)^{1} = 1.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{2(0.5)^2}{2(0.5)^1} = 0.5.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }2(0.5)^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-0.5} \\  & =\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation With an Arbitrary Starting Index
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $2.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

In this case, the first term is $a_2,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_2}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}=\frac{4}{9} \\ {a}_{3} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}=\frac{8}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{8}{27}\right)}{\left( \dfrac{4}{9}\right)} = \dfrac 2 3
$$

So, the sum of the series is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(1-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3}{9} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Non-Standard Form Using Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ In this case, the first term is $a_3,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

Computing the first few terms, we get:

$$
a_3 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(3)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}
$$

 

$$
a_4 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(4)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{8} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_4}{a_3} = \dfrac{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}}{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5{(\frac{1}{2})}^{7}}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{5}{128})}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =(\frac{5}{128})(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3(32)} \\  & =\frac{5}{96}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to evaluate the infinite geometric series 
 

$$
\sum_{n = 1} ^ \infty  3 \left (\dfrac 1 4\right) ^ n.
$$

The sum $S_\infty$ of an infinite geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_{\infty} = \dfrac {\color{black}a_1} {1 - {\color{black}r}},
$$

where ${\color{black}r}$ is the common ratio and $\color{black}a_1$ is the first term. So, we need to determine $\color{black}a_1$ and $\color{black}r$ and then plug those values into this formula.

The first term is

$$
{\color{black}a_1} = 3 \left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1 = {\color{black}\dfrac 3 4},
$$

and the common ratio is 

$$
{\color{black}r} = \dfrac {a_2}{\color{black}a_1} = \dfrac {3 \left (\dfrac 1 4 \right)^2}{3\left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1}= {\color{black}\dfrac 1 4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
